messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Tran is a thirty-one-year-old married man of Southeast Asian descent who serves as a judge in a busy metropolitan courthouse. Two years ago, during an especially severe monsoon season, a flash flood overwhelmed the city’s drainage system and swept through the downtown area without warning. Minh was in his chambers reviewing case files when the emergency sirens began to wail. Within minutes, water surged through the ground floor, cutting off power and trapping him and several colleagues on the upper levels. He remembers the exact moment the water first appeared at the base of the stairwell—a single, frozen image burned into his mind. That snapshot, vivid and perfectly preserved, is still the way the event comes back to him: not as a narrative but as a series of still pictures, each one as real as the moment it happened. He can feel the cold water climbing his legs, hear the shouts of a bailiff trying to keep everyone calm, and smell the muddy, metallic tang of the floodwater mixed with the gasoline and debris. When rescue arrived, he was loaded into an inflatable boat and taken to a field hospital set up in a nearby school gymnasium. The antiseptic smell of the medical tent, the sound of ambulance engines idling, and the sight of the rain-slicked streets all lodged themselves in his memory.

In the weeks and months that followed, Minh tried to push the event out of his mind. He told himself it was over, that he was safe now, and that the best thing was simply not to think about it. But the memories refused to stay buried. They returned not as ordinary recollections but as full sensory relivings: the floodwater rising around his desk, the metallic taste of panic, the pressure of bodies pushing toward the roof access. Each memory arrived as a discrete moment, a snapshot he could see in his mind’s eye—the face of the injured clerk, the red cross on the ambulance door, the waterline on the courthouse wall. He found himself avoiding relaxing, even at home. The moment he sat down to watch television or read a book, a tightness would spread across his chest. He had come to believe that lowering his guard was dangerous, that if he let himself feel calm, something terrible would happen again. He began to suppress any thought of the trauma as soon as it surfaced, but the suppression only made the images leap back with more force.

Minh’s daily life as a judge became a minefield. Ambulance sirens passing the courthouse sent a jolt through his body, making his hands tremble on the bench. The antiseptic smell from the cleaning crew became unbearable; he had to have the building’s janitorial products switched to unscented alternatives, yet even a faint chemical whiff from a courtroom’s hand sanitizer would trigger a rush of dread. Weather became his most constant threat monitor. Overcast skies, a drop in barometric pressure, or the sound of rain against the courthouse windows would make him feel as if the water was about to pour through the doorways again. He started to avoid going out whenever the forecast looked threatening. He would find reasons to stay inside the courthouse’s interior, windowless chambers, or work from home on days when storms were predicted. His wife noticed he had stopped agreeing to weekend outings or visits to her family if there was even a remote chance of precipitation. She felt he was pulling away, and he could not explain the panic that rose in his throat at the thought of being caught outside in a downpour.

The consequences crept into his professional life as well. He began delegating courtroom observations and site visits to other judges, claiming scheduling conflicts. His colleagues noticed, though they did not press. One afternoon, during a routine hearing, a sudden thunderstorm broke directly over the courthouse. The crack of lightning and the roar of rain against the windows sent Minh into a complete sensory reliving. For several seconds he was back in the flood, his breath short, his skin cold, the antiseptic smell of the hospital flooding his nose. He stopped speaking mid-sentence, gripped the edge of the bench, and called an abrupt recess. That evening, shaking in his chambers, he finally admitted to his wife that he needed help.

What brought Minh to therapy was that moment of paralysis in the courtroom. He is terrified that the memories are getting stronger, that they will eventually derail his career or destroy his marriage. He is afraid that talking about the trauma will make it worse, that he will drown in the snapshots all over again. But he is also desperate to sit through a rainy day without his mind filling with images of rising water, to hear a siren without his heart pounding, and to feel safe enough to relax in his own home. He does not know if that is possible, but he is willing to try.
